POST-WAR GROWTH IN POPULATION AND ITS CHARACTER

—A glance at the census figures gives a graphic picture of the growth of Fannin County following the Civil War. In 1860 the County population was 9,217; by 1870 it had reached 13,207; and during the next two decades it almost tripled, going from about 20,000 as the population was reported in 1880 and "over 40,000" by 1888. The rapid increase in population had brought in a varied family of the period. Most families had from six to eight children, families of ten children were not uncommon, and many had even more. But an equally important factor was the amount and character of the population. Like any of the less than most Southern states the economic destituteness of the war, and to many a young man who returned from the War for the Lost Cause to find his home in ruins and his financial resources gone, the opportunity of the Red River appeared as a promising land of new hope, and thither they greatly emigrated. Biographies make clear that the greatest number of Texas settlers who built up the social and economic foundation of the area brought their families from the older Southern states.

From the typical biographies it is seen that this element in the growing population of Fannin County was not of the ordinary pioneering adventurer type. Most of them, having the best culture of the Old South and were from families where good education and some wealth had prevailed. In many cases the war had interrupted the school or college career in the making of the student; there was no inclination to keep from the children what the parents had missed. Indeed, quite commonly the lack of completed education was the earnest motivation for seeing that his child should have it.
